generatedProse.concept-context: In psychology, presentations are a familiar form of assessment. You might present a study you have read, a small piece of your own analysis, or a poster at a conference-style session. The point is the same: you communicate an argument or set of findings clearly to an audience, usually with slides. A psychology presentation develops the academic voice the discipline prizes, and the clear communication that research and professional work demand.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two psychology students given the same brief: a ten-minute presentation on a study from their module.

Tom treats the task as reading out information. He copies his notes onto slides and plans to read them aloud, line by line, covering the method and results. The study is described, but the audience is left reading dense slides while Tom reads too. His presentation is really a document read out, not a talk. This misses what a presentation is for.

Amara treats the task as communicating a point to an audience. She works out one clear message about what the study shows, chooses what the audience needs to hear, and uses her slides to support the spoken argument rather than carry it. Her talk has a shape and a purpose. This is what an academic presentation is: a spoken argument, made clearly to listeners.

Both had the same brief. Only Amara understood that a presentation is communication to an audience, not a document read aloud.
generatedProse.summary: An academic presentation in psychology is a spoken piece of assessed work in which you communicate an argument or findings to an audience, usually with slides. It develops your academic voice and builds transferable skills such as clear communication. You can now explain what a presentation is, give an example of a skill it builds, and recognise the main types used for assessment. The next lessons turn this into practice: how you plan and structure a presentation, and how you design its visual aids.

check.body: In the worked example, what did Amara understand that Tom did not?

items.text: That a presentation is communication to an audience, not a document read aloud.
That more slides always make a presentation better.
That the study should be described as quickly as possible.
That reading notes aloud word for word is the safest approach.

feedback.correct: That's right. Amara understood a presentation is communication to an audience.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Amara grasped about the purpose of a presentation.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara understood a presentation is communication to an audience, not a document read aloud. The other options mistake slides, speed or reciting for the point.
